source: Jakubuv & Urban (2017) ENIGMA: Efficient Learning-based Inference Guiding Machine
finding: A fast learned classifier of 'will this clause appear in a proof' added to E's given-clause choice beat E's own tuned strategies on the CASC 2016 AIM set.
numbers: Train: 1020 problems; E auto-schedule solves 261, best single strategy 239, learned strategies together solve 337 at 30 s. Test: 200 problems, 180 s. ENIGMA total 52, one strategy 41, Vampire 47. With boosting of rare positive clauses: 57 solved, 16 not solved by Vampire; positive-class accuracy 12.5% to 81.8% while overall accuracy 98% to 93%.
limits: One narrow family (AIM, algebra, single source). Overall accuracy 97.6% hid very poor recall on useful clauses. Best strategies mix learned and hand-made queues. Gains came after retraining on solved proofs.
agent_relevance: Judge a clause scorer by recall on the rare useful clauses, not accuracy. Keep a plain baseline queue mixed in.

source: Loos, Irving, Szegedy, Kaliszyk (2017) Deep Network Guided Proof Search
finding: First deep nets (CNN, WaveNet) inside E's clause selection on Mizar. Network alone was too slow and lost the proof; a two-phase switch (network first, then fast heuristics) worked.
numbers: Mizar FOL: 57,882 theorems, 32,521 (56%) have an ATP proof; 25,361 'hard' ones were the test. Unguided 2.33% proved; simple CNN with switch 4.34% (86% more). All methods union 1,866 = 7.36%. Hold-out 50-50 clause accuracy: CNN 81.5%, WaveNet 640 78.7%.
quote: if we spend half of the time guiding the search and spend the rest finishing from that starting point
limits: WaveNet had better offline proxy metrics but the simple CNN won on actual proofs. Pure network guidance processed about 1% as many clauses as heuristics in the same time. On the easy set (96.6% already solved) gains were minor.
agent_relevance: Cheap scorer plus a handoff to a fast default beats an expensive scorer used throughout. Test the scorer inside the loop, not on a proxy.

source: Chvalovsky, Jakubuv, Suda, Urban (2019) ENIGMA-NG
finding: Gradient-boosted trees and a recursive neural net replaced ENIGMA's linear model in E. Trees won in real time; the neural net was competitive only after caching.
numbers: 10 s limit, baseline S 1086 problems. Best S+Mtree 1256 = +15.7%; tree is 3.8% above the best linear model (1210); neural S+Mnn 1197 (about +10%). 232 newly solved problems; on those, models lose about 15% true-positive and 20% true-negative rate. NN speed 6-7% of S; without caching its relative figure drops from 7.1 to 3.6.
limits: Same Mizar-style corpus family as Loos. Learned models cost evaluation time; the winner is chosen by solved problems under a clock.
agent_relevance: The cost of calling the scorer is part of its value. Cache and batch scoring calls.

source: Suda (2021) Improving ENIGMA-Style Clause Selection While Learning From History
finding: Ported learned clause selection to Vampire on SMT-LIB problems. Using the net as the only queue failed; it worked as a second layer of Vampire's queue mix.
numbers: Baseline 756 solved (734 on rerun). Single queue M1,0: 190 (25%). Layered S+S[M1] 1:1: 1032 (136%), 411 gained, 113 lost. Without abstraction caching 1007; without lazy evaluation 905 (119%); neither 782 (103%), 73% of time spent evaluating. Abstract: 41% improvement on a relevant SMT-LIB subset.
limits: Net trained on the same benchmark family (80/20 split of mini-batches). Replacing the queue outright did far worse than baseline.
agent_relevance: Learned selection is a strong addition and a poor replacement: keep age/weight queues alive.

source: Jakubuv et al. (2020) ENIGMA Anonymous: Symbol-Independent Inference Guiding Machine
finding: Symbol-independent features and GNN guidance in E on 57,880 Mizar40 problems. Trees again beat GNN in real time despite higher GNN recall on held-out clauses.
numbers: Real time 10 s: baseline 14,966; best tree D2 24,347 (+62.7%); best GNN N2 23,262 (+55.4%). Abstract time (5000 clauses): D2 +112.2%, N2 +107.6%. Portfolio with 8 more strategies solves 29,130, of which 2,109 are hard Mizar40.
limits: Training data comes from E's own earlier proofs on the same corpus, so large gains partly reflect in-distribution learning.
agent_relevance: Best learned guidance lives in a portfolio of complementary strategies.

source: Crouse et al. (2019) A Deep RL Approach to First-Order Logic Theorem Proving (TRAIL)
finding: RL from scratch inside a saturation prover (Beagle) beats earlier RL provers but still loses to E.
numbers: M2k: TRAIL 1,561; E 1,922; Beagle 1,543; plCop about 1,359. MPTP2078: TRAIL 910; E 998; Beagle 742 (22% relative gain); plCop about 782. Transfer: train MPTP, test M2k lost 11%; reverse lost 3%.
limits: plCop figures derived from the stated gaps (202 and 128). Best of 10 iterations is reported, so mild optimism.
agent_relevance: Learned control still trails a hand-tuned loop; keep a safe fallback.

source: Janota et al. (2022) Machine Learning Meets The Herbrand Universe
finding: A GNN2RNN proposes ground instances for a ground solver. A self-improving loop finds more proofs than random instantiation.
numbers: 113,332 clausal Mizar problems; 96,532 training. Random instantiator: 9,923 solved in 100 runs. Learned: 10,543 in 42 rounds. Test: 10.59% solved vs 3.3% for one random run.
limits: Instantiation route, not resolution. Random baseline is weak and absolute rates are low.
agent_relevance: Guess instances, then check with a cheap exact solver: a generate-and-verify pattern.

source: Wikipedia: Resolution (logic)
finding: Resolution with factoring is sound and refutation-complete. Robinson's unification (1965) removed the combinatorial explosion of Davis-Putnam (1960) by instantiating on demand.
numbers: Dates: Davis-Putnam 1960, Robinson 1965, Murray 1979-82, Nieuwenhuis-Rubio 2001. Listed provers: Otter, Prover9, SNARK, SPASS, Vampire, CARINE, GKC.
limits: Encyclopedic; no complexity results or benchmark numbers on the page.
agent_relevance: Completeness says a proof exists in the closure, not that a bounded search finds it. The control loop decides.

source: Olausson et al. (2023) LINC: Language Models with First-Order Logic Provers
finding: LLM translates to FOL; Prover9 (a resolution prover) decides; majority vote over 10 samples. Big gains for small models, none for GPT-4 on FOLIO.
numbers: FOLIO (182 clean examples): StarCoder+ 56.0% vs 41.8% best control; GPT-3.5 62.6% vs 54.9%; GPT-4 LINC 72.5% vs CoT 75.3%. ProofWriter (360 balanced): GPT-3.5 96.4%, GPT-4 98.3%; GPT-4 about 26 points above CoT. Syntax-error rate in FOL: 38% StarCoder+, 24% GPT-3.5, 13% GPT-4.
limits: 22 of 204 FOLIO items dropped for errors. LINC fails by omitting implicit facts so Prover9 says Uncertain; CoT fails by asserting a conclusion despite stated doubt.
agent_relevance: An exact prover as verifier is great where translation is easy; when world knowledge is implicit it is blind. Keep a free-reasoning fallback.

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM
finding: Solver offload with self-refinement; Prover9 for FOL. Gains largest where chain-of-thought is weak.
numbers: GPT-4 Standard / CoT / Logic-LM: ProofWriter 52.67 / 68.11 / 79.66; FOLIO 69.11 / 70.58 / 78.92; PrOntoQA 77.40 / 98.79 / 83.20 (solver worse than CoT); AR-LSAT 33.33 / 35.06 / 43.04. Average gain over CoT with GPT-4: 10.44 points.
limits: On PrOntoQA CoT beat Logic-LM. When the solver cannot run, results fall back to CoT, so numbers mix methods.
agent_relevance: The solver wins on non-linear problems (hypothesising, elimination) and loses on simple forward chains. Route by problem type.

source: Feng et al. (2023) Language Models can be Logical Solvers (LoGiPT)
finding: Fine-tune an LLM to emulate the solver's reasoning trace instead of calling the solver; avoids parse errors.
numbers: ProofWriter: best LoGiPT is 9.84 points absolute above Logic-LM (GPT-4, 79.66). Baselines: GPT-3.5 CoT 48.33 ProofWriter; vicuna-13b CoT 41.50 ProofWriter, 37.40 PrOntoQA.
limits: Trained on data close to the test style; mixing the two datasets lowered scores a few points. Synthetic deduction benchmarks only.
agent_relevance: A model can imitate a solver's trace, but that skill rides on matching the training format.

source: Ye, Chen, Dillig, Durrett (2023) SATLM
finding: LLM writes a declarative spec; an off-the-shelf solver (Z3) answers. Beats program-aided prompting on constraint-style tasks.
numbers: Beats program-aided LM by 23% on a hard GSM subset; GSM 84.8% with self-consistency; LSAT SOTA 30.9% to 37.4%; BoardgameQA 73.9% to 80.7%.
limits: SAT/SMT, not resolution; included as nearest cousin. Parse failures reduce coverage.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as LINC: errors move into the spec.

source: Haken (1985) The intractability of resolution
finding: Pigeonhole formulas need exponential-size resolution refutations. Recalled from memory, not opened this session.
numbers: No figure verified.
limits: Not opened; verify before citing.
agent_relevance: Completeness does not give speed; hard families exist where no clause-selection rule helps.

source: McCune (1997) Solution of the Robbins problem
finding: EQP, an equational prover, proved the Robbins conjecture. Recalled from memory, not opened.
numbers: No figures verified.
limits: Not opened; verify before citing.
agent_relevance: A saturation prover can solve open problems when strategy is tuned by hand for the domain.

source: Cross-reading: ENIGMA 2017, Loos 2017, ENIGMA-NG 2019, Suda 2021, ENIGMA Anonymous 2020
finding: Across five papers, learned guidance never worked as a full replacement of the prover's queues. Every success mixes learned and default queues.
numbers: Suda: net-only 25% of baseline; layered mix 136%. Loos: network phase then switch to heuristics. ENIGMA: best strategy mixes S0 with learned weight at frequency 30. ENIGMA-NG and Anonymous: S+M mixes.
limits: Each paper used its own corpus; percentages are not comparable across papers.
agent_relevance: Learned scorer as a minority queue next to a plain one.

source: Cross-reading: ENIGMA-NG vs ENIGMA Anonymous (accuracy versus solved)
finding: Neural models with better held-out recall lost to boosted trees in real-time solving in two separate papers.
numbers: ENIGMA-NG: Mtree 1256 vs Mnn 1197. Anonymous: D2 24,347 vs N2 23,262 though GNN TPR 90-92% vs tree TPR about 80%.
limits: Gap narrows in abstract time (equal clause budget), so loss is mostly evaluation cost.
agent_relevance: Measure under a fixed compute budget that includes scorer cost.

source: Loos et al. (2017) premise selection and clause guidance combined
finding: Premise selection and clause guidance were complementary: combining them gave the union of proved theorems.
numbers: Union of all combinations in Table 4: 1,712 (6.8%); neural-guided methods 1,665 (6.6%); with non-switched variants 1,866 (7.36%).
limits: Hard-statement set only. Individual table cells were garbled in text extraction; totals checked.
agent_relevance: Layered control: select premises first, then guide the loop.

source: Jakubuv & Urban (2017) ENIGMA training-data feedback
finding: Adding proofs found by the first learned run to the training data raised the ceiling further.
numbers: Added 52 competition proofs to 337 training solves; retrained model solved 5 more (4 not solved by Vampire), all within 45 s; total 57.
limits: Small numbers (200 problems); gains per round shrink.
agent_relevance: Learning from own successes is a loop with diminishing returns: plan a stop rule.

source: Crouse et al. TRAIL: processed clauses in the state
finding: Including the processed-clause set in the state gave a 6% relative gain on MPTP2078 and none on M2k.
numbers: M2k 1,561 both ways; MPTP2078 910 with processed clauses vs 854 without (56 more).
limits: No variance across seeds reported.
agent_relevance: Give the scorer the current set state, not only the candidate.

source: Suda (2021) threshold sweep for trusting the classifier
finding: Thresholds from -0.5 to 0 perform alike; above 0.25 performance falls.
limits: One benchmark and one model.
agent_relevance: Use a soft preference, not a hard filter.

source: Olausson et al. LINC depth analysis
finding: With LINC, accuracy falls as proof depth rises for the smallest model; CoT falls to chance above depth 1 for GPT-3.5.
numbers: StarCoder+ stays above chance but drops with depth; GPT-3.5 CoT equals chance within 1 SD at higher depth.
limits: ProofWriter only; per-bar numbers not read.
agent_relevance: Long deductive chains are where free-text reasoning breaks first.

source: Pan et al. Logic-LM reasoning-depth analysis
finding: Solver advantage over CoT grows with reasoning depth.
numbers: Logic-LM beats CoT by 7.1, 5.0, 12.7, 20.0 and 39.4 points at depth 0, 1, 2, 4, 5 (ProofWriter).
limits: Synthetic rules, one dataset.
agent_relevance: Route deep chains to a solver.

source: Pan et al. Logic-LM execution rates and self-refinement
finding: Translation is the weak link: near 100% executable on easy sets, low on hard ones. Self-refinement from solver errors helps modestly.
numbers: FOLIO GPT-3.5 executable 79.9% to 85.8% after refinement; AR-LSAT 32.6% to 39.8%; ProofWriter GPT-3.5 87.3% before.
limits: GPT-4 FOLIO executable rate not separately read.
agent_relevance: Feed solver error messages back for repair, but expect only a few points.

source: Feng et al. LoGiPT merged-data result
finding: Training one model on both ProofWriter and PrOntoQA slightly lowered accuracy versus separate training.
numbers: ProofWriter: merged 79.33 and 79.00 vs 81.17 single (vicuna-13b).
limits: Only open 13B models; gaps small.
agent_relevance: Format mismatch costs a few points even when the logic is the same.

source: Ye et al. SATLM declarative versus procedural prompting
finding: Declarative prompting adds value over regex-style program prompting.
numbers: Program style 37.1% vs declarative 44.0% on one task; with self-consistency it passes the previous best 55.6%.
limits: Task name not recorded in notes.
agent_relevance: Describe the problem, let the solver search.
